decks.title: System of Particles and Rotational Motion — Part 1: Centre of mass, torque and angular momentum
goals: Locate the centre of mass of simple systems and describe its motion under external forces
Define torque and angular momentum and relate them by τ = dL/dt
Apply conservation of angular momentum to simple situations

slides.narration: A cricket bat, a spinning skater and a firework shell are all systems of many particles. In this part we find the single point that represents the motion of the whole system, the centre of mass, and then meet torque and angular momentum, the rotational partners of force and momentum.

slides.heading: Centre of mass of a system of particles
slides.body_md: For particles of masses $m_1, m_2, \dots$ at positions $x_1, x_2, \dots$ along a line, the **centre of mass** (CM) is the mass-weighted average position.
bullets: For two particles the CM lies on the line joining them, **nearer the heavier one**, and divides the line in the inverse ratio of the masses.
In a plane (or in space) each coordinate is averaged separately.
The CM is a definite point of the system: choosing another origin changes its coordinates, not the point.
The CM need not coincide with any particle, or even with any material of the body.

math: x_\text{cm} = \dfrac{m_1 x_1 + m_2 x_2 + \cdots}{m_1 + m_2 + \cdots} = \dfrac{\sum m_i x_i}{M}
X = \dfrac{\sum m_i x_i}{M}, \qquad Y = \dfrac{\sum m_i y_i}{M}
slides.narration: To find the centre of mass, multiply each mass by its position, add these up, and divide by the total mass. It is a weighted average, so it is pulled towards the heavier particles. For two particles it lies on the line joining them, closer to the heavier one. It is a point of the system, whichever origin we choose to measure from.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: two masses on a rod
slides.body_md: Two small masses of $2.0$ kg and $6.0$ kg are fixed to the ends of a light rod $0.80$ m long. Find the centre of mass.
bullets: Take the origin at the $2.0$ kg mass: $x_1 = 0$ and $x_2 = 0.80$ m.
$x_\text{cm} = \dfrac{2.0 \times 0 + 6.0 \times 0.80}{8.0} = \dfrac{4.8}{8.0} = 0.60$ m from the lighter mass.
It is $0.20$ m from the heavier mass: the distances are in the inverse ratio of the masses.
Check: the weights balance about the CM, $19.6 \times 0.60 = 58.8 \times 0.20 \approx 11.8$ N m.

slides.narration: Put the origin at the lighter mass. Multiply six kilograms by zero point eight metres to get four point eight, divide by the total mass of eight kilograms, and the centre of mass is zero point six metres from the lighter mass. It is only zero point two metres from the heavier one, so the distances are in the inverse ratio of the masses.

slides.heading: Centre of mass of a rigid body
slides.body_md: A rigid body is a continuous collection of particles, so the sum becomes an integral. For uniform bodies **symmetry** gives the answer directly.
bullets: If a uniform body has a centre, an axis or a plane of symmetry, the CM lies on it (at the centre for a rod, disc, sphere or rectangle).
A ring or a hollow shell has its CM at the geometric centre, where there is no material.
A composite body: treat each simple part as a particle at its own CM, with the part’s mass.
Near the Earth’s surface the weight of a body acts through its CM (more on this in Part 2).

headers: Where the centre of mass is
rows: The centre of the ring; there is no material there
Where the medians meet, one third of the height above the base

visual.alt: Table of the position of the centre of mass of uniform bodies: rod, ring, disc, sphere, rectangular plate and triangular plate

slides.narration: For a uniform body with a line or a point of symmetry, the centre of mass lies on that line or at that point. A rod has it at the midpoint, a rectangular plate where the diagonals cross, a ring at its centre where there is no material at all. For a composite body, treat each simple piece as a particle at its own centre of mass.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: three particles in a plane
slides.body_md: Three small masses of $2.0$, $3.0$ and $5.0$ kg are fixed to a light frame at $(0, 0)$, $(4, 0)$ and $(0, 6)$, in metres. Find the CM.
bullets: $X = \dfrac{\sum m_i x_i}{M} = \dfrac{12}{10} = 1.2$ m.
$Y = \dfrac{\sum m_i y_i}{M} = \dfrac{30}{10} = 3$ m.
The CM is at (1.2 m, 3.0 m), pulled towards the heaviest particle.

visual.alt: Table of three particles with their masses and coordinates and the sums of mass times x and mass times y

slides.narration: Work out mass times x and mass times y for each particle and add. The sums are twelve and thirty kilogram metres. Dividing by the total mass of ten kilograms gives the centre of mass at one point two metres along x and three point zero metres along y, pulled towards the heaviest particle.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a bent wire
slides.body_md: A uniform wire is bent into an L with arms of $0.60$ m and $0.40$ m along the x and y axes from the corner. Find its CM.
bullets: The wire is uniform, so the mass of each arm is proportional to its length and acts at its midpoint.
Arm 1: length $0.60$ m, midpoint $(0.3, 0)$. Arm 2: length $0.40$ m, midpoint $(0, 0.2)$.
The point (0.18 m, 0.08 m) is not on the wire: the CM can lie outside the material.

slides.heading: Motion of the centre of mass
slides.body_md: Add Newton’s second law for all the particles. The forces between the particles come in equal and opposite pairs and cancel, leaving only external forces.
bullets: The CM moves as if all the mass were concentrated there and all the external force were applied there.
Internal forces (an explosion, a spring, muscles) cannot change the motion of the CM.
If the net external force is zero, the total momentum $\vec P$ is constant: the CM stays at rest or moves with constant velocity.
A thrown spanner or a shell bursting in flight: the CM follows the same path as a single particle would.

slides.narration: Adding Newton’s second law for every particle, the internal forces cancel in pairs. What is left says that the centre of mass moves as if all the mass were there and all the external force acted there. An explosion or a spring cannot change this motion. With no external force, the total momentum stays constant.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a shell bursts in flight
slides.body_md: A shell of mass $5.0$ kg moves horizontally at $20$ m s$^{-1}$ at the top of its path and bursts into two pieces. The $2.0$ kg piece continues horizontally at $45$ m s$^{-1}$. Find the speed of the other piece and describe the CM.
bullets: The burst forces are internal, so momentum along the horizontal is conserved: $5.0 \times 20 = 100$ kg m s$^{-1}$ before.
After: $100 = 2.0 \times 45 + 3.0\,v_2$, so $v_2 = \dfrac{10}{3.0} \approx 3.33$ m s$^{-1}$, in the same direction.
The CM keeps moving at $20$ m s$^{-1}$: after $3.0$ s the pieces are $135$ m and $10.0$ m ahead, and $\dfrac{2.0 \times 135 + 3.0 \times 10.0}{5.0} = 60.0$ m $= 20 \times 3.0$ m.
Both pieces start with zero vertical velocity, so they fall together and the CM follows the original parabola.

visual.alt: Horizontal distance against time for the two pieces of a shell after it bursts: the 2.0 kg piece at 45 metres per second, the 3.0 kg piece at 3.33 metres per second, and the centre of mass moving steadily at 20 metres per second between them
visual.caption: The CM keeps moving as if no burst had happened.

slides.narration: Momentum is conserved because the burst forces are internal. Before the burst it is one hundred kilogram metres per second. The two kilogram piece carries ninety, so the three kilogram piece carries ten, a speed of about three point three three metres per second. The centre of mass between them keeps moving at twenty metres per second, exactly as before the burst.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: a child walks on a sledge
slides.body_md: A child of $30$ kg stands at one end of a $2.4$ m long sledge of mass $90$ kg on smooth ice, everything at rest. She walks to the other end. How far does the sledge slide?
bullets: No external horizontal force acts, so the CM of child + sledge stays at the same place.
Let the sledge slide back by $s$. The child moves $2.4 - s$ relative to the ice.
Mass × displacement balances: $30\,(2.4 - s) = 90\,s$, so $s = \dfrac{30 \times 2.4}{120} = 0.60$ m.
The child moves $2.4 - 0.60 = 1.8$ m over the ice. Check: $30 \times 1.8 = 90 \times 0.60$.

slides.heading: Torque: the turning effect of a force
slides.body_md: A force $\vec F$ applied at position $\vec r$ from an axis has a **torque** (moment of force) $\vec\tau = \vec r \times \vec F$.
bullets: $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec r$ and $\vec F$; $d = r \sin\theta$ is the **perpendicular distance** from the axis to the line of action of the force.
Direction: along the axis, by the right-hand rule; for a body turning in a plane, anticlockwise is taken as positive.
SI unit: newton metre (N m). It has the same dimensions as energy but is a different quantity.
The torque is zero if $F = 0$, or if the line of action passes through the axis ($\theta = 0$ or $180^\circ$).
Pushing at the end of a long handle, at right angles to it, gives the largest torque for a given force.

Its size is the force times the perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of action, which is the same as the distance to the point of application times the force times the sine of the angle between them. A force whose line of action passes through the axis has no turning effect.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: a bicycle pedal
slides.body_md: A cyclist pushes a pedal straight down with $300$ N. The crank is $0.17$ m long. Find the torque about the axle when the crank makes $60^\circ$ with the vertical, and compare other positions.
bullets: The angle between the crank ($\vec r$) and the downward force is $\theta = 60^\circ$.
$\tau = r F \sin\theta = 0.17 \times 300 \times \sin 60^\circ \approx 44.2$ N m, with moment arm $d = 0.17 \sin 60^\circ \approx 0.147$ m.
With the crank vertical (θ = 0) the line of action passes through the axle and the torque is zero; with the crank horizontal (θ = 90°) the torque is greatest.

visual.alt: Table of the moment arm and torque of a 300 newton downward pedal force on a crank 0.17 metres long at four crank angles

slides.narration: The crank and the force make an angle of sixty degrees. The torque is the crank length, zero point one seven metres, times the force, three hundred newtons, times the sine of sixty degrees. That is about forty four newton metres. At zero degrees the torque vanishes, and at ninety degrees it reaches its largest value, fifty one newton metres.

slides.heading: Angular momentum and its link with torque
slides.body_md: For a particle of momentum $\vec p$ at position $\vec r$ from a point O, the **angular momentum** is $\vec l = \vec r \times \vec p$, magnitude $m v r \sin\theta = m v d$.
bullets: Unit: kg m$^2$ s$^{-1}$. For circular motion about the centre, $l = m v r = m r^2 \omega$.
For a particle, the torque of the force on it equals the rate of change of its angular momentum; for a system, only **external** torques change the total $\vec L$ (internal torques cancel in pairs).
The relation is the rotational form of Newton’s second law, just as $\vec F = d\vec p/dt$.

headers: Rotational motion about a point or axis
rows: angular momentum l = r × p, magnitude m v r sin θ

visual.alt: Table comparing momentum with angular momentum, force with torque, and the two conservation laws

slides.narration: The angular momentum of a particle about a point is its position vector crossed with its momentum. Its size is mass times speed times the perpendicular distance from the point to the line of motion. The torque on the particle equals the rate of change of this angular momentum, which is the rotational form of Newton's second law.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: a particle on a straight line
slides.body_md: A $0.50$ kg ball moves at a steady $8.0$ m s$^{-1}$ along a straight line that passes $3.0$ m from a point O. Find its angular momentum about O.
bullets: Where the ball is, it is at a larger distance $r$ from O but the angle changes so that $r\sin\theta$ stays equal to $d$.
No force acts, so the torque about O is zero and L is the same at every position: A, B or C.
The direction of L is perpendicular to the plane containing O and the line, and does not change.

slides.heading: Conservation of angular momentum
slides.body_md: If the net external torque on a system is zero, $d\vec L/dt = 0$: the total angular momentum stays **constant**.
bullets: When the body can change its shape, a smaller moment of inertia I means a larger angular speed ω, and the reverse.
A skater or dancer pulls the arms in to spin faster; a diver tucks to somersault; a person on a rotating stool pulls weights inward.
A helicopter needs a tail rotor: the main rotor’s angular momentum has to be balanced so that the body does not spin the other way.
The Earth, a planet or a comet moving under a force directed towards the Sun feels no torque about the Sun, so its angular momentum stays constant.

slides.heading: Worked example 8: a rotating stool
slides.body_md: A student on a frictionless rotating stool holds two $1.5$ kg weights at $0.80$ m from the axis, turning at $3.0$ rad s$^{-1}$. Her body and the stool have a moment of inertia $0.60$ kg m$^2$. She pulls the weights in to $0.20$ m. Find the new angular speed.
bullets: No external torque: $I_1\omega_1 = I_2\omega_2$, so $\omega_2 = \dfrac{2.52 \times 3.0}{0.72} = 10.5$ rad s$^{-1}$.
$L = 2.52 \times 3.0 = 7.56$ kg m$^2$ s$^{-1}$ before and after: the spin is about 3.5 times faster.

That is ten point five radians per second, three and a half times faster.

slides.body_md: Key results:

rows: X = Σ m x / M; nearer the heavier mass; may lie outside the body
M a_cm = F_ext; internal forces cannot change it
P constant; the CM moves uniformly or stays at rest
τ = r × F; magnitude r F sin θ = F d; unit N m
l = r × p; magnitude m v d; unit kg m² s⁻¹; τ = dL/dt
L constant: I ω stays the same

visual.alt: Summary table of the centre of mass, its motion, torque, angular momentum and the conservation laws

slides.narration: To sum up. The centre of mass is the mass weighted average position of the system. It moves as if all the mass were there and only external forces acted on it. Torque is force times perpendicular distance. The torque on a system equals the rate of change of its angular momentum, and when there is no external torque the angular momentum stays constant.

slides.narration: A plank over a drain, a signboard on a bracket and a spinning grinding wheel all depend on one idea: how forces and torques act on a rigid body. In this part we find when a body stays in equilibrium, then meet the moment of inertia, the rotational counterpart of mass.

slides.heading: Equilibrium of a rigid body
slides.body_md: A rigid body is in **mechanical equilibrium** when both its translation and its rotation are unchanging.
bullets: The first condition says the CM has zero acceleration; the second says the angular momentum is not changing.
Each condition can hold without the other: two equal and opposite forces along different lines give zero net force but a torque (a couple).
If the net force is zero, the net torque is the same about every point, so the point for taking moments may be chosen freely.
Choose the point where an unknown force acts: that force then has no moment and drops out of the equation.

rows: The centre of mass has no acceleration
Sum of external torques = 0 (about any point)
The body has no angular acceleration
At rest if it started at rest

visual.alt: Table of the conditions for translational, rotational and mechanical equilibrium of a rigid body

slides.narration: A rigid body is in mechanical equilibrium when the sum of the external forces is zero and the sum of the external torques is zero. Either can hold without the other, for example with two equal and opposite forces along different lines. When the net force is zero, the torque is the same about every point, so we may take moments about whichever point removes an unknown force.

slides.heading: Principle of moments
slides.body_md: For a body in rotational equilibrium about a point, the **sum of the clockwise moments equals the sum of the anticlockwise moments** about that point.
bullets: A carrying pole with $18$ kg and $12$ kg loads balances where $18\,g \times x = 12\,g \times (1.5 - x)$, so $x = 0.60$ m from the heavier load.
The shoulder then supports the whole weight, $(12 + 18) \times 9.8 = 294$ N.
The balance point of loads on a light pole is the centre of mass of the loads.
The principle works for any lever: effort × effort arm = load × load arm, with the arms measured perpendicular to the forces.

slides.heading: Centre of gravity and stability
slides.body_md: The **centre of gravity** (CG) is the point through which the total weight of the body acts; the torque of the weights of all its particles about the CG is zero.
bullets: When g is the same at all parts of the body, which is true for ordinary bodies, the CG coincides with the centre of mass.
A body is balanced if it is supported at its CG, or if the support force acts along the vertical line through the CG.
A body is **stable** while the vertical line through its CG falls inside its base; it topples when the line leaves the base.
A low CG and a wide base make a body more stable: a loaded roof rack raises the CG and a lorry topples more easily.

The cable’s moment is $T \sin 30^\circ \times 1.2$, so $T \times 0.60 = 23.52 + 23.52 = 47.04$.
Hinge force: horizontal $T\cos 30^\circ \approx 67.9$ N away from the wall; vertical $(58.8 - 39.2) = 19.6$ N upward.

slides.heading: A couple
slides.body_md: Two **equal, opposite and parallel** forces whose lines of action differ form a **couple**.
bullets: The net force of a couple is zero, so it cannot accelerate the CM; it only turns the body.
Its torque is the same about every point: $F$ times the perpendicular distance $d$ between the two lines.
Twisting the lid of a jar with two fingers, or turning a key, applies a couple; a single force would also push the body sideways.
To keep a body in equilibrium a couple must be balanced by an equal and opposite couple, not by a single force.

rows: F × (distance between the lines), the same about every point
Turns it without moving its centre of mass

visual.alt: Table comparing a single force with a couple: net force, net torque and effect

slides.narration: A couple is a pair of equal and opposite parallel forces that do not lie on the same line. The net force is zero, so the centre of mass does not accelerate, but there is a torque equal to the force times the distance between the lines. That torque is the same about every point. A couple can only be balanced by another couple.

slides.body_md: Choose the correct option.

rows: The centre of mass has no acceleration

slides.narration: Check the sum of the forces and the sum of the torques separately.

slides.heading: Moment of inertia
slides.body_md: The **moment of inertia** measures a body’s resistance to a change in its rotation about an axis. For particles it is the sum of mass times the square of the distance from the axis.
bullets: For a rigid body the sum becomes an integral; the answer depends on the mass, on where the mass is (distance from the axis) and on the axis chosen.
The same body has different values of I about different axes.
It is the rotational counterpart of mass: for a given torque, a larger I gives a smaller angular acceleration.
Mass far from the axis counts for much more than mass near it, because r is squared.

rows: How the mass is distributed (distance from the axis)
The position and direction of the axis
Whether the body is turning at all

visual.alt: Table of what the moment of inertia of a body depends on and what it does not depend on

slides.narration: The moment of inertia of a set of particles about an axis is the sum of each mass times the square of its distance from the axis. It depends on the mass, on how that mass is spread out, and on the axis. Mass far from the axis counts much more because the distance is squared. It plays the role that mass plays in linear motion.

slides.heading: Worked example 11: four masses on a square frame
slides.body_md: Four masses of $0.50$ kg each are fixed at the corners of a light square frame of side $0.60$ m. Find the moment of inertia about the axis through the centre perpendicular to the frame, and the radius of gyration.
bullets: Each corner is at distance $r = \dfrac{0.60}{\sqrt{2}}$ from the centre, so $r^2 = \dfrac{0.60^2}{2} = 0.18$ m$^2$.
$I = \sum m r^2 = 4 \times 0.50 \times 0.18 = 0.36$ kg m$^2$.
The **radius of gyration** $k$ is defined by $I = M k^2$, with $M = 2.0$ kg: $k = \sqrt{\dfrac{0.36}{2.0}} \approx 0.424$ m, which here equals $r$ because all the mass is at the same distance.

visual.alt: Table of four equal masses at the corners of a square frame with each distance from the central axis, its square and mass times distance squared, totalling 0.36

slides.narration: Each corner is the same distance from the centre, so the square of that distance is half the square of the side, zero point one eight square metres. Four masses of half a kilogram give a moment of inertia of zero point three six kilogram metre squared. The radius of gyration, found from the moment of inertia divided by the total mass, is about zero point four two four metres.

slides.heading: Moments of inertia of simple bodies, and radius of gyration
slides.body_md: For the standard uniform bodies of mass $M$ and radius $R$, about an axis through the centre, the values (stated, not derived) are $I = c\,M R^2$.
bullets: Ring or hollow cylinder (about its axis): $c = 1$; hollow sphere (about a diameter): $c = \tfrac{2}{3}$; disc or solid cylinder (about its axis): $c = \tfrac{1}{2}$; solid sphere (about a diameter): $c = \tfrac{2}{5}$.
Thin rod of length $L$ about an axis through its centre perpendicular to it: $I = \tfrac{1}{12} M L^2$.
**Radius of gyration** $k = \sqrt{I/M}$: the distance at which the whole mass would have to be placed to give the same I. For a ring $k = R$; for a disc $k = R/\sqrt{2}$.
For the same mass and radius a ring has the largest I of the four because all its mass is at the greatest distance.

A thin rod about its centre has one twelfth of mass times length squared. The radius of gyration is the square root of the moment of inertia divided by the mass.

slides.heading: Worked example 12: a ring and a disc
slides.body_md: A ring and a disc each have mass $8.0$ kg and radius $0.25$ m. Find the moment of inertia and the radius of gyration of each about its axis.
bullets: Disc: $I = \tfrac{1}{2} M R^2 = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 8.0 \times 0.25^2 = 0.250$ kg m$^2$; $k = \dfrac{R}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 0.177$ m.
The ring has twice the moment of inertia: it is twice as hard to start or stop turning.

visual.alt: Table of the moment of inertia and radius of gyration of a ring and a disc of the same mass and radius

slides.narration: For the ring the moment of inertia is mass times radius squared, which is half a kilogram metre squared. The disc has half of that, zero point two five. The radius of gyration of the ring equals its radius, while that of the disc is smaller, about zero point one eight metres. So the ring is twice as hard to start or stop turning.

slides.heading: Rotation about a fixed axis: torque, angular momentum and energy
slides.body_md: For a rigid body turning about a fixed axis with angular velocity $\omega$, each particle has speed $v = r\omega$.
bullets: Angular momentum about the axis: $L = \sum m r^2 \omega = I \omega$.
Newton’s second law for rotation: $\tau = I\alpha$ with $\alpha = d\omega/dt$ the angular acceleration; the greater I, the smaller α for the same torque.
Kinetic energy: $K = \sum \tfrac{1}{2} m v^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}(\sum m r^2)\omega^2 = \tfrac{1}{2} I \omega^2$, the rotational analogue of $\tfrac{1}{2} m v^2$.
A flywheel has its mass near the rim so that I is large: it stores more energy at a given ω and smooths the motion.

visual.alt: Table of the correspondence between linear quantities and rotational quantities about a fixed axis

slides.narration: For a rigid body turning about a fixed axis, each particle moves at its distance times the angular velocity. Adding up gives angular momentum equal to I omega, torque equal to I times angular acceleration, and kinetic energy equal to half I omega squared. Each is the rotational twin of a linear relation, with moment of inertia taking the place of mass.

slides.heading: Worked example 13: energy in a grinding wheel
slides.body_md: A grinding wheel is a uniform disc of mass $12$ kg and radius $0.20$ m turning at $600$ revolutions per minute. Find its kinetic energy.
bullets: $\omega = \dfrac{2\pi \times 600}{60} \approx 62.83$ rad s$^{-1}$.
$K = \tfrac{1}{2} I \omega^2 = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 0.24 \times 62.83^2 \approx 474$ J.
Doubling ω would make K four times as large.

functions.label: K = ½ I ω², I = 0.24 kg m²

visual.alt: Kinetic energy of a grinding wheel against angular speed: a parabola, reaching about 474 joules at 62.8 radians per second
visual.caption: Rotational kinetic energy grows as the square of ω.

slides.narration: First the moment of inertia of the disc: half of twelve times the radius squared, which is zero point two four kilogram metre squared. Six hundred revolutions per minute is about sixty two point eight radians per second. Half I omega squared then gives about four hundred and seventy four joules. Doubling the angular speed would make the energy four times larger.

slides.heading: Worked example 14: a constant torque on a flywheel
slides.body_md: A flywheel of moment of inertia $2.0$ kg m$^2$ starts from rest and a constant torque of $6.0$ N m acts on it for $5.0$ s. Find its angular momentum, angular speed and kinetic energy at the end.
bullets: $\tau = dL/dt$ is constant, so $L = \tau t = 6.0 \times 5.0 = 30$ kg m$^2$ s$^{-1}$.
$\omega = \dfrac{L}{I} = \dfrac{30}{2.0} = 15$ rad s$^{-1}$ (the angular acceleration is $\tau/I = 3.0$ rad s$^{-2}$).
$K = \tfrac{1}{2} I \omega^2 = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 2.0 \times 15^2 = 225$ J, equal to the work done by the torque.

The kinetic energy is half of two times fifteen squared, two hundred and twenty five joules, which equals the work done by the torque.

sections.heading: 1. Centre of mass and its motion
sections.body_md:
- The **centre of mass** (CM) of particles is the mass-weighted average position: $X = \sum m_i x_i / M$, and likewise for $Y$. For two particles it lies on the line joining them, nearer the heavier one; the distances are in the inverse ratio of the masses.
- Masses $2.0$ kg and $6.0$ kg at the ends of a light $0.80$ m rod: CM at $0.60$ m from the lighter mass.
- For uniform rigid bodies symmetry decides: midpoint of a rod, centre of a ring, disc or sphere, crossing of the diagonals of a rectangle. A composite body is treated as particles at the CMs of its parts. A wire bent into an L (arms 0.60 m and 0.40 m) has its CM at (0.18 m, 0.08 m): not on the wire.
- **Motion of the CM:** $M\vec a_\text{cm} = \vec F_\text{ext}$ and $\vec P = M\vec v_\text{cm}$. Internal forces cancel in pairs and cannot change it. With no external force the CM stays at rest or moves uniformly.
- A shell bursting in flight: the CM keeps its path. A child walking on a free sledge of 90 kg moves 1.8 m while the sledge slides back 0.60 m.

key_terms.definition_md: The point whose position is the mass-weighted average of the positions of all the particles; it moves as if all the mass and all the external force were there.
A force between two parts of the same system; such forces occur in equal and opposite pairs.

sections.heading: 2. Torque and angular momentum
sections.body_md:
- **Torque** $\vec\tau = \vec r \times \vec F$; magnitude $\tau = rF\sin\theta = Fd$, where $d$ is the perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of action. Unit N m. Anticlockwise is taken as positive for motion in a plane. A force through the axis has zero torque.
- A 300 N downward pedal force on a 0.17 m crank at 60° from the vertical gives 44.2 N m.
- **Angular momentum** of a particle $\vec l = \vec r \times \vec p$, magnitude $mvd$ (unit kg m² s⁻¹); for a circle $l = mvr = mr^2\omega$. A ball of 0.50 kg at 8.0 m s⁻¹ along a line 3.0 m from O has $L = 12.0$ kg m² s⁻¹ at every position.
- $\vec\tau_\text{ext} = d\vec L/dt$ (internal torques cancel in pairs). If $\tau_\text{ext} = 0$, $L$ is constant: **conservation of angular momentum**.
- Examples: a dancer or a person on a stool pulling the weights in (I falls from 2.52 to 0.72 kg m², ω rises from 3.0 to 10.5 rad s⁻¹); a diver tucking; a helicopter’s tail rotor; a planet under a central force.

key_terms.definition_md: The turning effect of a force about an axis: force times the perpendicular distance from the axis to its line of action.
The vector r × p of a particle about a point; for a rigid body about a fixed axis, I ω.

sections.heading: 3. Equilibrium of rigid bodies and centre of gravity
sections.body_md:
- A rigid body is in **mechanical equilibrium** when $\sum\vec F_\text{ext} = 0$ (translational) and $\sum\vec\tau_\text{ext} = 0$ (rotational). If the net force is zero, the net torque is the same about every point, so take moments where an unknown force acts.
- **Principle of moments:** clockwise moments = anticlockwise moments about any point. A light carrying pole with 18 kg and 12 kg loads balances 0.60 m from the heavier load.
- A uniform 4 m plank of 30 kg on end supports with a 50 kg person 1 m from one end: supports 514.5 N and 269.5 N ($g = 9.8$ m s⁻²). A hinged bar with a cable at 30°: $T = 78.4$ N.
- A **couple** (equal, opposite, parallel forces on different lines) has zero net force and torque $F\times d$, the same about every point.
- **Centre of gravity:** the point where the weight acts; it coincides with the CM when g is uniform over the body. A body is stable while the vertical through its CG falls inside the base; a 0.6 m wide, 1.8 m tall almirah topples at a tilt of about 18.4°.

key_terms.definition_md: For rotational equilibrium the sum of the clockwise moments about a point equals the sum of the anticlockwise moments.
Two equal, opposite, parallel forces with different lines of action; it produces rotation without translation.
The point through which the whole weight of a body acts.

sections.heading: 4. Moment of inertia, radius of gyration and rotational energy
sections.body_md:
- **Moment of inertia** $I = \sum m_i r_i^2$ (kg m²): it depends on the mass, how it is distributed and the axis. Four 0.50 kg masses at the corners of a 0.60 m square about the central perpendicular axis: $I = 0.36$ kg m².
- **Radius of gyration** $k = \sqrt{I/M}$, so $I = Mk^2$.
- Values about an axis through the centre (stated, not derived): ring or hollow cylinder $MR^2$; hollow sphere $\tfrac{2}{3}MR^2$; disc or solid cylinder $\tfrac{1}{2}MR^2$; solid sphere $\tfrac{2}{5}MR^2$; thin rod about its centre, perpendicular, $\tfrac{1}{12}ML^2$. For 8 kg and 0.25 m: ring 0.500, disc 0.250 kg m².
- Fixed axis: $L = I\omega$, $\tau = I\alpha$, $K = \tfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2$. A grinding wheel (12 kg, 0.2 m) at 600 rev/min has 474 J. A torque of 6 N m for 5 s on I = 2 kg m² gives ω = 15 rad s⁻¹.
- Not included here: the parallel and perpendicular axes theorems and rolling motion, which the rationalised book does not require.

key_terms.definition_md: The sum of mass times the square of the distance from the axis; the rotational counterpart of mass.
The distance k from the axis at which the whole mass M would give the same moment of inertia, I = M k².

notes.exam_tips_md:
- Say which point or axis a torque, angular momentum or moment of inertia refers to.
- Find the perpendicular distance (or the sine of the angle) before multiplying force by distance.
- For equilibrium write both conditions and take moments about the point with the most unknown forces.
- Use "no external force, so the centre of mass is unchanged" and "no external torque, so L is constant" explicitly.
- Convert revolutions per minute to radians per second (multiply by 2π/60) before using K = ½ I ω².

cards.front_md: Write the centre of mass of particles along a line.
cards.back_md: $x_\text{cm} = \sum m_i x_i / M$, the mass-weighted average position.

cards.front_md: Where does the CM of two particles lie?
cards.back_md: On the line joining them, nearer the heavier one; distances are in the inverse ratio of the masses.

cards.front_md: Masses 2.0 kg and 6.0 kg at the ends of a 0.80 m light rod: where is the CM?
cards.back_md: 0.60 m from the 2.0 kg mass.

cards.front_md: Where is the CM of a uniform ring?
cards.back_md: At its centre, where there is no material.

cards.front_md: Can the CM of a body lie outside the body?
cards.back_md: Yes, for a ring or a bent wire, for example.

cards.front_md: State the equation of motion of the CM.
cards.back_md: $M\vec a_\text{cm} = \vec F_\text{ext}$: only external forces matter.

cards.front_md: Why can internal forces not change the CM motion?
cards.back_md: They occur in equal and opposite pairs that cancel in the sum.

cards.front_md: A shell bursts in flight. How does its CM move?
cards.back_md: As if no burst had occurred (same path), until a piece meets an outside force.

cards.front_md: What is the total momentum of a system in terms of its CM?
cards.back_md: $\vec P = M\vec v_\text{cm}$.

cards.front_md: Write the magnitude of the torque of a force.
cards.back_md: $\tau = rF\sin\theta = Fd$.

cards.front_md: What is d in torque?
cards.back_md: The perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of action of the force.

cards.front_md: SI unit of torque?
cards.back_md: Newton metre (N m).

cards.front_md: When is the torque of a force zero?
cards.back_md: When F = 0 or the line of action passes through the axis.

cards.front_md: Define the angular momentum of a particle.
cards.back_md: $\vec l = \vec r \times \vec p$, magnitude $mvd$.

cards.front_md: SI unit of angular momentum?
cards.back_md: kg m² s⁻¹.

cards.front_md: Relate torque and angular momentum.
cards.back_md: $\vec\tau_\text{ext} = d\vec L/dt$.

cards.front_md: State the law of conservation of angular momentum.
cards.back_md: If the net external torque is zero, the total angular momentum is constant.

cards.front_md: Why does a dancer spin faster when she pulls in her arms?
cards.back_md: I falls while L = Iω stays constant, so ω rises.

cards.front_md: State the two conditions of mechanical equilibrium.
cards.back_md: Sum of external forces = 0 and sum of external torques = 0.

cards.front_md: State the principle of moments.
cards.back_md: In rotational equilibrium, clockwise moments equal anticlockwise moments about any point.

cards.front_md: What is a couple?
cards.back_md: Two equal, opposite, parallel forces on different lines: zero net force, torque F × d.

cards.front_md: Define the centre of gravity.
cards.back_md: The point through which the whole weight of the body acts.

cards.front_md: When do the CG and the CM coincide?
cards.back_md: When g is the same over the whole body (the usual case).

cards.front_md: When does a body topple?
cards.back_md: When the vertical line through its CG falls outside its base.

cards.front_md: Define the moment of inertia of particles.
cards.back_md: $I = \sum m_i r_i^2$, unit kg m².

cards.front_md: Define the radius of gyration.
cards.back_md: $k = \sqrt{I/M}$, so $I = Mk^2$.

cards.front_md: I of a ring about its axis? Of a disc?
cards.back_md: Ring $MR^2$; disc $\tfrac{1}{2}MR^2$.

cards.front_md: I of a solid sphere about a diameter?
Write the rotational analogue of F = ma.
cards.back_md: $\tau = I\alpha$.

cards.front_md: Write the kinetic energy of rotation about a fixed axis.
cards.back_md: $K = \tfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2$ with ω in rad s⁻¹.

questions.stem_md: Two beads of mass 3.0 kg and 1.0 kg are fixed on a light straight wire, 0.40 m apart. Their centre of mass lies

options.text_md: 0.10 m from the 1.0 kg bead
0.20 m from each bead, at the midpoint
0.10 m from the 3.0 kg bead, on the wire between them
0.30 m from the 3.0 kg bead

questions.solution_md: Take the 3.0 kg bead as origin: x_cm = (3.0 × 0 + 1.0 × 0.40)/4.0 = 0.10 m. The CM is nearer the heavier bead — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A thin steel bangle of uniform thickness lies flat on a table. Its centre of mass is located

options.text_md: at the point of the bangle nearest the table edge
on the circumference, at the heaviest point
at the geometric centre of the bangle, in the empty space inside it
at no point, because a bangle has no centre of mass

questions.solution_md: By symmetry the CM of a uniform ring is at its centre, where there is no material — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A uniform tent pole of constant thickness is balanced on a single finger. The finger has to be placed at the ___ of the pole.
questions.solution_md: The CM of a uniform rod is at its **midpoint**; supporting it there balances the weight.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The centre of mass of a rigid body always coincides with some particle of the body.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. For a ring, a hollow sphere or a bent wire the CM lies in empty space; it is a point defined by the mass distribution.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A firework shell bursts at the top of its flight and throws fragments in many directions, yet the centre of mass of all the fragments continues along the original parabola until one of them lands.

**Reason (R):** The forces of the burst are internal to the system, so the only external force is gravity.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true, and R explains A: internal forces cannot change the motion of the CM, which therefore follows the path set by gravity alone — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Two bumper cars on a straight fairground track move towards each other: a 200 kg car at +6.0 m/s and a 300 kg car at −4.0 m/s. The velocity of their centre of mass is

options.text_md: zero: the centre of mass is at rest
+1.0 m/s, the mean of the two velocities
+2.4 m/s, towards the heavier car’s start

questions.solution_md: v_cm = (200 × 6.0 + 300 × (−4.0))/500 = (1200 − 1200)/500 = 0. The momenta cancel, so the CM is at rest — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In a carbon monoxide molecule the carbon atom (mass 12 u) and the oxygen atom (mass 16 u) are 0.113 nm apart. Find the distance of the centre of mass from the carbon atom, in nm (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: Origin at the carbon atom: $x_\text{cm} = \dfrac{12 \times 0 + 16 \times 0.113}{12 + 16} = \dfrac{1.808}{28} = 0.0646$ nm, towards the heavier oxygen atom.

marking_scheme.step: Weighted average with origin at carbon

questions.stem_md: Three small beads of mass 4.0 kg, 1.0 kg and 3.0 kg lie on a flat tray at (0, 0), (5.0 m, 0) and (2.0 m, 6.0 m). Find the y-coordinate of their centre of mass, in m.
questions.solution_md: $Y = \dfrac{4.0 \times 0 + 1.0 \times 0 + 3.0 \times 6.0}{4.0 + 1.0 + 3.0} = \dfrac{18}{8.0} = 2.25$ m. (The x-coordinate is 1.375 m.)

marking_scheme.step: Y = Σ m y / Σ m

questions.stem_md: A uniform wire 1.00 m long is bent at its midpoint into a right angle, so each arm is 0.50 m. Find the distance of its centre of mass from the corner, in m (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: Arms along x and y from the corner, each of equal mass at its midpoint (0.25 m from the corner): $X = Y = \dfrac{0.50 \times 0.25}{1.00} = 0.125$ m. Distance $= \sqrt{0.125^2 + 0.125^2} = 0.177$ m.

marking_scheme.step: Each arm acts at its midpoint with equal mass: X = Y = 0.125 m

questions.stem_md: The Earth (mass 6.0 × 10²⁴ kg) and the Moon (mass 7.35 × 10²² kg) have their centres 3.84 × 10⁸ m apart. Find the distance of their common centre of mass from the Earth’s centre, in km (3 significant figures), and say whether it lies inside the Earth (radius 6400 km).
questions.solution_md: $x_\text{cm} = \dfrac{m\,d}{M + m} = \dfrac{7.35 \times 10^{22} \times 3.84 \times 10^{8}}{6.0 \times 10^{24} + 7.35 \times 10^{22}} \approx 4.647 \times 10^{6}$ m $= 4647$ km. This is less than 6400 km, so it lies inside the Earth.

marking_scheme.step: x_cm = m d/(M + m) from the Earth’s centre

questions.stem_md: A girl of mass 45 kg stands at one end of a 135 kg trolley, 3.2 m long, on the smooth floor of a railway workshop; both are at rest. She walks to the other end of the trolley. Find the distance moved by the trolley over the floor, in m.
questions.solution_md: No external horizontal force acts, so the CM does not move. If the trolley moves $s$ backwards, the girl moves $3.2 - s$ forwards over the floor: $45(3.2 - s) = 135\,s$. So $s = \dfrac{45 \times 3.2}{180} = 0.800$ m.

marking_scheme.step: CM fixed: m (L − s) = M s

questions.stem_md: A shell of mass 8.0 kg flying horizontally at 30 m/s bursts into two pieces. A 3.0 kg piece continues in the same direction at 70 m/s. Find the velocity of the other piece, in m/s (positive in the original direction).
questions.solution_md: The burst forces are internal, so momentum is conserved: $8.0 \times 30 = 3.0 \times 70 + 5.0\,v$. So $v = \dfrac{240 - 210}{5.0} = 6.00$ m/s in the original direction.

questions.stem_md: Two blocks of 2.0 kg and 3.0 kg on a smooth horizontal table are joined by a stretched spring. Outside pushes act along the line of the spring: 10 N eastwards on the 2.0 kg block and 5.0 N westwards on the 3.0 kg block. Find the acceleration of the centre of mass, in m/s² (east positive).
questions.solution_md: The spring forces are internal. $a_\text{cm} = \dfrac{F_\text{ext}}{M} = \dfrac{10 - 5.0}{2.0 + 3.0} = 1.00$ m/s² eastwards.

questions.stem_md: From a uniform square plate of side 0.40 m a square of side 0.20 m is cut out at one corner. Taking the cut corner of the original plate as the origin, with x along one side, find the x-coordinate of the centre of mass of the remaining plate, in m (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: Treat the removed square as a negative mass. Areas (proportional to mass): full plate $0.16$ m² at $x = 0.20$ m; removed piece $0.04$ m² at $x = 0.10$ m. $X = \dfrac{0.16 \times 0.20 - 0.04 \times 0.10}{0.16 - 0.04} = \dfrac{0.028}{0.12} = 0.233$ m.

marking_scheme.step: Whole plate minus the removed part, mass ∝ area

questions.stem_md: What is meant by the centre of mass of a system of particles? Give an example of a body whose centre of mass lies outside the body.

answer.model_answer_md: The centre of mass is the point whose position is the mass-weighted average of the positions of all the particles, $\sum m_i \vec r_i / M$; the system moves as if all its mass and external force were there. A uniform ring or a bent wire has it in empty space, at the centre of the ring.

questions.solution_md: Weighted average position; ring example.

marking_scheme.step: Mass-weighted average position Σ m r / M

questions.stem_md: A passenger sits in a car standing on frictionless ice and pushes hard on the dashboard with both hands. Will the centre of mass of the car and passenger move? Explain.

answer.model_answer_md: No. The push and the dashboard’s reaction are internal forces of the system, equal and opposite, and the ice exerts no horizontal force. With no external horizontal force the centre of mass stays at rest; the car and passenger may only shift relative to each other.

questions.solution_md: Internal forces only.

marking_scheme.step: Push and reaction are internal and cancel; no external horizontal force
So the CM stays at rest (only relative shift)

questions.stem_md: Show that the total momentum of a system of particles equals $M\vec v_\text{cm}$, and hence that the centre of mass moves with constant velocity when no external force acts.

answer.model_answer_md: The centre of mass is defined by $M\vec r_\text{cm} = \sum m_i \vec r_i$, where $M$ is the total mass. Differentiating once with respect to time gives $M\vec v_\text{cm} = \sum m_i \vec v_i$, which is the total momentum $\vec P$ of the system. Differentiating again gives $M\vec a_\text{cm} = d\vec P/dt = \vec F_\text{ext}$, because the internal forces cancel in equal and opposite pairs. When no external force acts, the acceleration of the centre of mass is zero, so its velocity stays constant.

questions.solution_md: Differentiate the CM definition twice.

marking_scheme.step: Differentiate M r_cm = Σ m r once: P = M v_cm
Differentiate again: M a_cm = F_ext (internal forces cancel)

questions.stem_md: (a) Write the position of the centre of mass of two particles of masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ at $x_1$ and $x_2$. [1] (b) Show that $M\vec a_\text{cm} = \vec F_\text{ext}$ for a system of particles. [2] (c) Two trolleys on a smooth horizontal rail, 4.0 kg at 3.0 m/s and 6.0 kg at 1.0 m/s, move in the same direction. Find the velocity of their centre of mass, and their common speed if they lock together after a collision. [2]

answer.model_answer_md: (a) For two particles the centre of mass is at $x_\text{cm} = \dfrac{m_1x_1 + m_2x_2}{m_1 + m_2}$, the mass-weighted average of the two positions. (b) Write Newton’s second law for every particle, $m_i\vec a_i = \vec F_i^\text{ext} + \sum_j \vec F_{ij}$, and add the equations. The internal forces satisfy $\vec F_{ij} = -\vec F_{ji}$, so they cancel in pairs and leave only the external forces; and since the sum of $m_i\vec a_i$ is $M\vec a_\text{cm}$, we get $M\vec a_\text{cm} = \vec F_\text{ext}$. (c) The velocity of the centre of mass is $\dfrac{4.0 \times 3.0 + 6.0 \times 1.0}{10} = 1.80$ m/s. The collision forces are internal and no external force acts, so the velocity of the centre of mass is unchanged: the locked trolleys move together at 1.80 m/s.

questions.solution_md: Weighted average; internal forces cancel; v_cm constant.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Sum of Newton’s second law; internal pairs cancel

questions.stem_md: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.
questions.passage_md: A craft shop in Jaipur sells a hanging decoration made of a light rod 1.00 m long with three brass bells fixed to it. The bells have masses 0.10 kg, 0.30 kg and 0.20 kg, at 0 m, 0.40 m and 1.00 m from the left end. The decoration is hung from a single thread tied at the point where the rod stays horizontal.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (b) the centre of mass of the three bells, because the total weight then has no turning effect about it

**(b)** 0.533 m

**(c)** (i) The masses are now 0.30 kg at 0 m, 0.30 kg at 0.40 m and 0.20 kg at 1.00 m, total 0.80 kg. $x_\text{cm} = \dfrac{0 + 0.12 + 0.20}{0.80} = 0.400$ m, so the tying point moves towards the left end.

**OR** (ii) The claim is **wrong**. The rod is light, so its own weight is negligible and the centre of mass is set by the bells, which are not placed symmetrically. The thread must go at the centre of mass of the bells, here 0.533 m from the left end, not at the midpoint.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** The thread supports the whole weight along its line; for balance this line must pass through the centre of mass of the system — option (b).

**(b)** $x_\text{cm} = \dfrac{0.10 \times 0 + 0.30 \times 0.40 + 0.20 \times 1.00}{0.60} = \dfrac{0.32}{0.60} = 0.533$ m.

**(c)** (i) Recompute the weighted average.

(ii) Light rod: CM set by the bells.

children.stem_md: The rod hangs horizontally when the thread is tied at

options.text_md: the midpoint of the rod, because the rod is light
the centre of mass of the three bells, because the total weight then has no turning effect about it
the heaviest bell, because it pulls hardest
the lightest bell, because it needs the most support

children.solution_md: The thread supports the whole weight along its line; for balance this line must pass through the centre of mass of the system — option (b).

children.stem_md: Find the distance of the tying point from the left end, in m (3 significant figures).
**Either** (i): A second 0.20 kg bell is added at the left end (0 m). Find the new tying point.

answer.model_answer_md: The masses are now 0.30 kg at 0 m, 0.30 kg at 0.40 m and 0.20 kg at 1.00 m, total 0.80 kg. $x_\text{cm} = \dfrac{0 + 0.12 + 0.20}{0.80} = 0.400$ m, so the tying point moves towards the left end.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): A student says the thread should always be tied at the midpoint (0.50 m) of the rod because the rod is uniform. Evaluate this claim.

answer.model_answer_md: The claim is **wrong**. The rod is light, so its own weight is negligible and the centre of mass is set by the bells, which are not placed symmetrically. The thread must go at the centre of mass of the bells, here 0.533 m from the left end, not at the midpoint.

alternatives.solution_md: Light rod: CM set by the bells.

marking_scheme.step: Claim wrong: the rod is light, the bells decide the CM
Thread at the CM of the bells, 0.533 m, not 0.50 m

questions.stem_md: A force of 30 N acts on the rim of a bicycle wheel that is free to turn about its axle. The torque of this force about the axle is zero when the force is

options.text_md: along the tangent to the rim
at 45° to the radius of the wheel
directed along a radius, towards or away from the axle
of any direction, if it is large enough

questions.solution_md: Torque = F d, where d is the perpendicular distance from the axle to the line of action. A radial force has a line of action through the axle, so d = 0 — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Which of these is the SI unit of the angular momentum of a spinning wheel?

options.text_md: kg m s⁻¹
kg m² s⁻³
kg m s⁻²
kg m² s⁻¹

questions.solution_md: L = m v r has units kg × (m s⁻¹) × m = kg m² s⁻¹ — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A diver leaves the board in the layout position with moment of inertia 14.0 kg m² about her somersault axis and an angular speed of 1.5 rad/s. She tucks, reducing the moment of inertia to 3.5 kg m². Her angular speed in the tuck is

options.text_md: 1.5 rad/s, unchanged
6.0 rad/s
0.38 rad/s
21 rad/s

questions.solution_md: Gravity gives no torque about her CM, so L = I ω is constant: ω₂ = 14.0 × 1.5/3.5 = 6.0 rad/s — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A diver who tucks her body in mid-air spins faster.

**Reason (R):** The weight of the diver exerts a torque about her centre of mass that increases her angular speed.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: with no external torque L = Iω is constant, and tucking reduces I. R is false: the weight acts at the centre of mass, so its torque about the CM is zero — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A cricket ball flies in a straight line at constant velocity (air resistance neglected). Its angular momentum about the wicket-keeper’s gloves stays constant.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. No force acts, so the torque about any point is zero and L = m v d is constant: the perpendicular distance d to the line of flight does not change.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The total angular momentum of a system can change even when the net external torque is zero, because its parts can exert torques on each other.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. Internal torques occur in equal and opposite pairs and cancel, so only an external torque can change the total angular momentum.

questions.stem_md: The rate of change of the total angular momentum of a system about a point equals the net ___ torque on it.
questions.solution_md: Only the **external** torque counts; internal torques cancel in pairs.

questions.stem_md: A bullock yoked at the end of a 2.5 m long horizontal pole turns a sugar-cane crusher (kolhu). It pulls with 420 N at 50° to the pole. Find the torque about the vertical axis, in N m (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $\tau = r F \sin\theta = 2.5 \times 420 \times \sin 50^\circ = 804$ N m.

marking_scheme.step: τ = r F sin θ with θ = 50°

questions.stem_md: A 0.25 kg rubber ball on a 0.80 m string is whirled in a horizontal circle at 6.0 m/s. Find its angular momentum about the centre of the circle, in kg m²/s.
questions.solution_md: The velocity is perpendicular to the radius, so $L = m v r = 0.25 \times 6.0 \times 0.80 = 1.20$ kg m$^2$/s.

questions.stem_md: A 0.16 kg cricket ball flies at a steady 30 m/s along a straight line that passes 1.2 m from a point O. Find its angular momentum about O, in kg m²/s (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $L = m v d = 0.16 \times 30 \times 1.2 = 5.76$ kg m$^2$/s, the same at every point of its flight.

marking_scheme.step: Perpendicular distance 1.2 m gives L = m v d

questions.stem_md: Under a constant torque the angular momentum of a flywheel about its axle rises from 4.0 kg m²/s to 16 kg m²/s in 3.0 s. Find the torque, in N m.
questions.solution_md: $\tau = \dfrac{\Delta L}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{16 - 4.0}{3.0} = 4.00$ N m.

questions.stem_md: A girl on a frictionless rotating stool holds two 2.0 kg weights 0.90 m from the axis and turns at 2.0 rad/s. Her body and the stool together have a moment of inertia 0.80 kg m². She pulls the weights in to 0.30 m from the axis. Find her new angular speed, in rad/s (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $I_1 = 0.80 + 2 \times 2.0 \times 0.90^2 = 4.04$ kg m$^2$ and $I_2 = 0.80 + 2 \times 2.0 \times 0.30^2 = 1.16$ kg m$^2$. With no external torque, $I_1\omega_1 = I_2\omega_2$: $\omega_2 = \dfrac{4.04 \times 2.0}{1.16} = 6.97$ rad/s.

questions.stem_md: A stationary wheel of moment of inertia 8.0 kg m² about its axle receives a constant torque of 12 N m for 4.0 s. Find its angular speed at the end of that time, in rad/s.
questions.solution_md: $L = \tau t = 12 \times 4.0 = 48$ kg m$^2$ s$^{-1}$ (starting from zero). $\omega = \dfrac{L}{I} = \dfrac{48}{8.0} = 6.00$ rad/s.

questions.stem_md: State the law of conservation of angular momentum and use it to explain why a Kathak dancer spins faster when she draws her outstretched arms close to her body.

answer.model_answer_md: If the net external torque on a system is zero, its total angular momentum stays constant. With the arms drawn in, the moment of inertia I decreases; since $L = I\omega$ is constant, the angular speed $\omega$ must increase.

questions.solution_md: No external torque: L constant; I down, ω up.

marking_scheme.step: Statement: no external torque, L constant
I decreases, so ω increases (Iω constant)

questions.stem_md: A single-rotor helicopter has a small rotor on its tail. Explain, using angular momentum, why the helicopter would spin without it.

answer.model_answer_md: Before take-off the angular momentum is zero. When the engine spins the main rotor one way, the rotor gains angular momentum; with no external torque the total must stay zero, so the body would spin the opposite way. The tail rotor’s thrust gives an opposing torque that stops this.

questions.solution_md: Conservation of L: body turns opposite to the rotor.

marking_scheme.step: Total L stays zero: rotor turns one way, body the opposite way

questions.stem_md: For a single particle of momentum $\vec p$ at position $\vec r$ from a point O, show that the torque of the force on it about O equals $d\vec l/dt$, where $\vec l = \vec r \times \vec p$.

answer.model_answer_md: Differentiate $\vec l = \vec r \times \vec p$ with the product rule: $\dfrac{d\vec l}{dt} = \vec v \times \vec p + \vec r \times \dfrac{d\vec p}{dt}$. The first term is zero, because the velocity is parallel to the momentum and a vector crossed with a parallel vector vanishes. In the second term Newton’s second law says that the rate of change of momentum is the force, so it equals $\vec r \times \vec F$, the torque of the force about O. Hence the torque equals the rate of change of the angular momentum.

questions.solution_md: Product rule; v × p = 0; dp/dt = F.

marking_scheme.step: v × p = 0 because p is parallel to v
dp/dt = F gives r × F = τ

questions.stem_md: A person on a frictionless rotating stool pulls two held weights towards the axis. State what happens to her angular speed and to the kinetic energy of rotation, and explain the source of any change in energy.

answer.model_answer_md: Her angular speed increases, because $I\omega$ is constant while $I$ decreases. The rotational kinetic energy can be written $K = L^2/2I$, so with $L$ constant and $I$ smaller, $K$ increases. The extra energy is not created: it comes from the work done by her muscles as they pull the weights inward against the pull needed to keep them moving in a circle.

questions.stem_md: (a) Define the torque of a force about a point and the angular momentum of a particle about a point, giving the SI unit of each. [2] (b) State the law of conservation of angular momentum and the condition for it. [1] (c) A 0.50 kg ball moves at 6.0 m/s along a straight line passing 2.0 m from a point O. Find its angular momentum about O. A constant net torque of 4.0 N m about O, in the sense of the angular momentum, then acts for 1.5 s; find the new angular momentum. [2]

answer.model_answer_md: (a) The torque of a force about a point is the cross product $\vec\tau = \vec r \times \vec F$, of magnitude $rF\sin\theta$ and unit newton metre. The angular momentum of a particle is the cross product $\vec l = \vec r \times \vec p$, of magnitude $mvr\sin\theta$ and unit kg m$^2$ s$^{-1}$. (b) When the net external torque on a system is zero, its total angular momentum remains constant. (c) The angular momentum is $L = mvd = 0.50 \times 6.0 \times 2.0 = 6.00$ kg m$^2$/s. The torque equals the rate of change of angular momentum, so the increase is torque times time, $4.0 \times 1.5 = 6.00$, and the new value is $6.00 + 6.00 = 12.0$ kg m$^2$/s.

questions.solution_md: Definitions; conservation law; L = m v d; ΔL = τ t.

questions.passage_md: A playground roundabout in a Bengaluru park has a moment of inertia 200 kg m² about its vertical axle and turns freely at 1.5 rad/s. A 30 kg child, running on the ground and moving radially inwards, steps gently on to the rim, which is 2.0 m from the axle. Treat the child as a point mass and neglect friction at the axle.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (d) the angular momentum about the axle, because the only forces are internal or pass through the axle

**(b)** 0.94 rad/s

**(c)** (i) Before the child steps on, the kinetic energy of rotation is $K_1 = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 200 \times 1.5^2 = 225$ J. After she is on the rim the moment of inertia is larger and the angular speed smaller, and the kinetic energy is $K_2 = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 320 \times 0.9375^2 \approx 140.6$ J. The roundabout therefore loses about 84.4 J of kinetic energy, which appears as heat at her feet.

**OR** (ii) The claim is **wrong**. Conservation of angular momentum needs only zero external torque; kinetic energy is conserved only if no energy is dissipated. The child’s feet slip on the rim in an inelastic way, so energy is lost as heat: here the kinetic energy falls from 225 J to about 141 J.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** No external torque about the axle acts, so the angular momentum is conserved. The step is inelastic, so the kinetic energy changes — option (d).

**(b)** $I' = 200 + 30 \times 2.0^2 = 320$ kg m$^2$. $200 \times 1.5 = 320\,\omega'$, so $\omega' = \dfrac{300}{320} = 0.94$ rad/s.

**(c)** (i) K = ½ I ω² before and after.

(ii) L conserved; K not, because the interaction is inelastic.

marking_scheme.step: Moments about the left end, plank weight at 1.5 m

questions.stem_md: Two children push in opposite directions at the two ends of a light bamboo pole lying on a smooth floor, each with a force of 25 N at right angles to the pole. The pole is then in

options.text_md: translational equilibrium but not rotational equilibrium
rotational equilibrium but not translational equilibrium
complete mechanical equilibrium
neither translational nor rotational equilibrium

questions.solution_md: The two forces are equal and opposite, so the net force is zero (translational equilibrium). They act along different lines, so they form a couple with a non-zero net torque; the pole starts to turn — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A porter balances a light bamboo pole 2.0 m long on his shoulder, with a 15 kg load at one end and a 5.0 kg load at the other. His shoulder must be placed

options.text_md: 0.50 m from the 5.0 kg load
1.0 m from either load, at the midpoint
1.5 m from the 15 kg load
0.50 m from the 15 kg load

questions.solution_md: Equal moments about the shoulder: 15 × x = 5.0 × (2.0 − x), so x = 10/20 = 0.50 m from the heavier load — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The centre of gravity of a body coincides with its centre of mass when

options.text_md: the acceleration due to gravity is the same at every part of the body
the body is made of a single material
the body is perfectly rigid, whatever the gravity
the body is at rest on the ground

questions.solution_md: The weight of each particle is m g; if g is the same for all particles, the weights are proportional to the masses and the point of action of the total weight is the CM — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A bullock cart carrying sacks of grain is likely to overturn on a sloping village road. The cart is made more stable against overturning by

options.text_md: piling the sacks high above the floor
narrowing the wheelbase to save space
loading the heavy sacks at the bottom and using a wider wheelbase
moving all the load to the top of one side

questions.solution_md: A lower centre of gravity and a wider base keep the vertical line through the CG inside the base up to a larger tilt — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A light beam rests on a single pivot with weights hung on either side and stays horizontal. The sum of the clockwise ___ about the pivot then equals the sum of the anticlockwise ones.
questions.solution_md: This is the principle of **moments** for rotational equilibrium.

questions.stem_md: True or false? If the net force on a rigid body is zero and the net torque about one point is zero, the net torque about every other point is also zero.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. With zero net force, shifting the reference point changes the total torque by (displacement) × (net force) = 0, so a body in equilibrium may have its moments taken about any convenient point.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A uniform plank placed on a single trestle exactly at its midpoint stays horizontal.

**Reason (R):** The weight of the plank acts at its centre of gravity, directly above the trestle, so its torque about the trestle is zero.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true and R explains A: with the whole weight acting through the point of support, there is no net torque about it — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A carpenter pulls the handle of a claw hammer with 40 N at right angles to it, 0.30 m from the pivot. The nail is held in the claw 0.06 m from the pivot. Find the force on the nail, in N.
questions.solution_md: Moments about the pivot: $F \times 0.06 = 40 \times 0.30$, so $F = \dfrac{12.0}{0.06} = 200$ N.

questions.stem_md: A uniform horizontal bar 1.0 m long and of mass 3.0 kg is hinged at a wall and held by a cable fixed to its free end, making 30° with the bar. A 1.0 kg board hangs from the free end. Find the tension in the cable, in N (g = 9.8 m/s²).
questions.solution_md: Moments about the hinge: $T \sin 30^\circ \times 1.0 = 3.0 \times 9.8 \times 0.50 + 1.0 \times 9.8 \times 1.0$. So $T \times 0.50 = 14.70 + 9.80 = 24.50$ and $T = \dfrac{24.50}{0.50} = 49.0$ N.

marking_scheme.step: Moments about the hinge with T sin 30° as the effective component

questions.stem_md: A uniform ladder 5.0 m long and of mass 20 kg leans against a smooth vertical wall with its foot 3.0 m from the wall, on rough ground. Find the force the wall exerts on the ladder, in N (g = 9.8 m/s²).
questions.solution_md: The ladder reaches a height $\sqrt{5.0^2 - 3.0^2} = 4$ m. Moments about the foot: the wall force (horizontal, at height 4 m) balances the weight $196$ N at horizontal distance $1.5$ m: $N \times 4 = 196 \times 1.5$. So $N = \dfrac{294.0}{4} = 73.5$ N.

marking_scheme.step: Height 4.0 m; moments about the foot

questions.stem_md: To open a jar, a person presses on opposite sides of its lid with two fingers, each pushing tangentially with 4.5 N in opposite directions. The lid has diameter 7.0 cm. Find the torque of this couple, in N m.
questions.solution_md: The two forces are 7.0 cm apart, so $\tau = F \times d = 4.5 \times 0.070 = 0.315$ N m.

marking_scheme.step: τ = F × distance between the lines of action

questions.stem_md: A uniform rod of mass 2.0 kg and length 1.0 m carries a small 3.0 kg weight fixed at one end. Find the distance from the free end at which the combination balances on a knife edge, in m.
questions.solution_md: Measure from the free end: the rod’s weight acts at $0.50$ m and the 3.0 kg weight at $1.0$ m. $x = \dfrac{2.0 \times 0.50 + 3.0 \times 1.0}{2.0 + 3.0} = \dfrac{4.0}{5.0} = 0.800$ m.

marking_scheme.step: Balance point = CG of rod and weight

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between translational and rotational equilibrium of a rigid body, stating the condition for each.

answer.model_answer_md: A body is in translational equilibrium when the vector sum of the external forces on it is zero, so its centre of mass has no acceleration. It is in rotational equilibrium when the sum of the external torques about any point is zero, so its angular momentum does not change.

questions.solution_md: Σ F = 0 and Σ τ = 0.

marking_scheme.step: Translational: Σ F = 0, no acceleration of the CM
Rotational: Σ τ = 0, no angular acceleration

questions.stem_md: Why is a lorry whose roof rack is piled high with luggage more likely to topple on a banked bend than the same lorry with the luggage on the floor?

answer.model_answer_md: Luggage on the roof raises the centre of gravity. The lorry topples once the vertical line through the centre of gravity falls outside the line joining the wheels. A higher centre of gravity reaches this limit at a smaller tilt, so the loaded lorry is less stable.

questions.solution_md: Higher CG: the plumb line leaves the base at a smaller tilt.

marking_scheme.step: Vertical through the CG leaves the base at a smaller tilt

questions.stem_md: State the two conditions for equilibrium of a rigid body. A light beam 2.0 m long rests on supports at its two ends and carries a 30 N load 0.50 m from the left support. Find the support forces.

answer.model_answer_md: The two conditions are that the sum of the external forces is zero and the sum of the external torques is zero. Taking moments about the left support removes its unknown force: $R_R \times 2.0 = 30 \times 0.50$, so $R_R = 7.50$ N. Balancing the vertical forces, the left support must supply the rest, $R_L = 30 - 7.50 = 22.5$ N; the support nearer the load carries more.

questions.solution_md: Moments about one support, then balance of forces.

marking_scheme.step: R_L = 22.5 N from the force balance

questions.stem_md: (a) State the conditions for a rigid body to be in mechanical equilibrium, and state the principle of moments. [2] (b) A uniform bar 2.0 m long, of mass 5.0 kg, is hinged to a wall and held horizontal by a cable fixed to its free end and making 45° with the bar. Take g = 9.8 m/s². Find the tension in the cable. [2] (c) Find the vertical component of the force exerted by the hinge. [1]

answer.model_answer_md: (a) A rigid body is in mechanical equilibrium when the vector sum of the external forces is zero and the sum of the external torques about any point is zero. The principle of moments says that the clockwise moments about a point equal the anticlockwise moments. (b) Take moments about the hinge, so the unknown hinge force drops out. Only the component $T \sin 45^\circ$ perpendicular to the bar has a moment, with arm 2.0 m, balancing the weight 49 N acting at the middle: $T \sin 45^\circ \times 2.0 = 5.0 \times 9.8 \times 1.0$, so $T \approx 34.6$ N. (c) For the vertical forces, $H_y + T\sin 45^\circ = 49$, so $H_y = 49 - 24.5 = 24.5$ N upward.

questions.solution_md: Moments about the hinge, then vertical balance.

questions.passage_md: A 5.0 m long uniform plank of mass 40 kg is laid across a drain. One support A is under its left end; the other support B is 4.0 m from the left end, so the right end of the plank overhangs B by 1.0 m. A 40 kg man stands at the right end of the plank. Take g = 9.8 m/s².

**(b)** 735 N

**(b)** Moments about A: $R_B \times 4.0 = 40 \times 9.8 \times 2.5 + 40 \times 9.8 \times 5.0$. So $R_B = \dfrac{980.0 + 1960}{4.0} = 735$ N.

questions.stem_md: A motor applies a constant torque of 18 N m to a flywheel of moment of inertia 6.0 kg m² about its axle, which is free to turn. Find the angular acceleration of the flywheel, in rad/s².
questions.solution_md: $\tau = I\alpha$, so $\alpha = \dfrac{\tau}{I} = \dfrac{18}{6.0} = 3.00$ rad/s$^2$.

questions.stem_md: A flywheel is spinning on its axle. Its moment of inertia about the axle does NOT depend on

options.text_md: the mass of the flywheel
the angular speed with which it is spinning
how the mass is distributed about the axle
the position of the axle chosen

questions.solution_md: I = Σ m r² depends on the masses, their distances from the axis and the axis chosen, not on how fast the body turns — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A thin brass ring and a solid brass disc have the same mass and the same radius. About the axis through the centre perpendicular to their planes, the moment of inertia of the ring is

options.text_md: half that of the disc
equal to that of the disc
four times that of the disc
twice that of the disc

questions.solution_md: Ring: M R². Disc: ½ M R². The ratio is 2 : 1 — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The radius of gyration of a rotating body about a given axis is

options.text_md: the distance of the centre of mass from the axis
the distance from the axis at which all the mass, concentrated at one place, would give the same moment of inertia
the largest distance of any particle from the axis
half the radius of the body

questions.solution_md: It is defined by I = M k², so k = √(I/M) — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A uniform circular potter’s disc is replaced by another of the same material and mass but twice the radius. About the central axis, its moment of inertia becomes

options.text_md: four times the earlier value
twice the earlier value
eight times the earlier value
unchanged, because the mass is the same

questions.solution_md: I = ½ M R² with M fixed: doubling R multiplies I by 2² = 4 — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A solid sphere and a hollow spherical shell have the same mass and radius. About a diameter, the ratio of the moment of inertia of the solid sphere to that of the shell is
questions.solution_md: Solid sphere (2/5) M R²; shell (2/3) M R². Ratio = (2/5)/(2/3) = 3/5 — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The SI unit of the moment of inertia of a spinning top is kg ___.
questions.solution_md: I = Σ m r², so its unit is kg **m²**.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A ring-shaped flywheel and a disc-shaped flywheel of the same mass and radius are spinning at the same angular speed. The ring stores more rotational kinetic energy.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. K = ½ I ω²; the ring has I = M R², twice the disc’s ½ M R², so at the same ω it stores twice the energy.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A uniform rod has the same moment of inertia about every axis, since its mass does not change with the axis.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. I = Σ m r² depends on the distances from the chosen axis; for example, for a thin rod I about its centre perpendicular to its length is M L²/12, while about the rod’s own length it is almost zero.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The moment of inertia of a rigid body is the same about every axis.

**Reason (R):** The moment of inertia is the sum of m r², where r is the distance of each particle from the axis.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false: r depends on the axis, so I does too. R is true: it is the definition of I — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The radius of gyration of a thin ring about its central axis is equal to its radius.

**Reason (R):** The radius of gyration of every rigid body equals the radius of the body.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: I = M R² gives k = R for a ring. R is false: for a disc k = R/√2 and for a solid sphere k = R√(2/5) — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The kinetic energy of a disc turning about its central axis is ½ I ω².

**Reason (R):** The kinetic energy of a body moving in a straight line is ½ m v².

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true, but R does not explain A: ½ I ω² follows from adding ½ m v² for every particle with v = r ω, not from the linear formula alone — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Four beads of mass 0.25 kg each are fixed at the corners of a light square frame of side 0.40 m. Find the moment of inertia about the axis through the centre of the frame perpendicular to its plane, in kg m² (2 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: Each bead is at $r = 0.40/\sqrt{2}$ from the centre, so $r^2 = \dfrac{0.40^2}{2} = 0.080$ m$^2$. $I = \sum m r^2 = 4 \times 0.25 \times 0.080 = 0.080$ kg m$^2$.

questions.stem_md: For the four-bead frame (total mass 1.0 kg, moment of inertia 0.080 kg m² about the central perpendicular axis), find the radius of gyration about that axis, in m (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $k = \sqrt{\dfrac{I}{M}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{0.080}{1.0}} = 0.283$ m, equal to the distance of each bead from the axis.

questions.stem_md: A cast-iron brake disc has mass 6.0 kg and radius 0.15 m. Treating it as a uniform solid disc, find its moment of inertia about its axle, in kg m² (3 significant figures).
A ring-shaped flywheel of mass 40 kg and radius 0.50 m turns at 600 revolutions per minute. Find its kinetic energy of rotation, in kJ (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $I = M R^2 = 40 \times 0.50^2 = 10$ kg m$^2$ and $\omega = \dfrac{2\pi \times 600}{60} \approx 62.83$ rad/s. $K = \tfrac{1}{2} I \omega^2 \approx \tfrac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 62.83^2 \approx 19740$ J $= 19.7$ kJ.

marking_scheme.step: I = M R² = 10 kg m²; ω = 2π n/60

questions.stem_md: Two 2.0 kg balls are fixed to the ends of a light rod 1.0 m long, which turns at 4.0 rad/s about a perpendicular axis through its midpoint. Find the kinetic energy of the system, in J.
questions.solution_md: Each ball is $0.50$ m from the axis, so $I = 2 \times 2.0 \times 0.50^2 = 1.00$ kg m$^2$. $K = \tfrac{1}{2} I \omega^2 = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 1.00 \times 4.0^2 = 8.00$ J.

marking_scheme.step: I = Σ m r² = 1.0 kg m²

questions.stem_md: A girl on a frictionless rotating stool turns at 2.0 rad/s with a total moment of inertia 4.04 kg m². She pulls two weights inwards, reducing the moment of inertia to 1.16 kg m². Find the increase in the kinetic energy of rotation, in J (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $\omega_2 = \dfrac{4.04 \times 2.0}{1.16} \approx 6.966$ rad/s. $K_1 = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 4.04 \times 2.0^2 = 8.08$ J and $K_2 = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 1.16 \times 6.966^2 \approx 28.14$ J. Increase $= 28.14 - 8.08 = 20.1$ J, supplied by her muscles.

questions.stem_md: A thin uniform rod of mass 1.2 kg and length 0.90 m is turned about an axis through its centre perpendicular to its length. Find its moment of inertia, in kg m² (2 significant figures).

marking_scheme.step: I = M L²/12 for a rod about its centre

questions.stem_md: Define the moment of inertia of a rigid body about an axis and state two factors on which it depends.

answer.model_answer_md: The moment of inertia is the sum of the products of the mass of each particle and the square of its perpendicular distance from the axis, $I = \sum m_i r_i^2$. It depends on the mass of the body, on how the mass is distributed about the axis, and on the position and direction of the axis.

questions.solution_md: I = Σ m r²; mass, distribution, axis.

marking_scheme.step: Two factors: mass distribution, axis chosen (or the mass)

questions.stem_md: The heavy flywheel of a diesel pump has most of its mass in a thick rim. Explain the advantage of this design.

answer.model_answer_md: Mass at the rim is far from the axis, and $I = \sum m r^2$, so the moment of inertia is large. A large $I$ means a large kinetic energy $\tfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2$ at a given speed and a small change of $\omega$ for a given torque, so the flywheel stores energy and keeps the motion steady.

questions.solution_md: Large I from rim mass: stores energy, smooths the speed.

marking_scheme.step: Rim mass gives a large I
Large I stores more energy and resists changes in ω

questions.stem_md: Name the rotational counterparts of mass, force and linear momentum, and write the rotational form of Newton’s second law for a body turning about a fixed axis.

answer.model_answer_md: Mass corresponds to the moment of inertia $I$, force to torque $\tau$, and linear momentum to angular momentum $L = I\omega$. The rotational form of Newton’s second law is $\tau = I\alpha$, where $\alpha$ is the angular acceleration.

questions.solution_md: I, τ, L; τ = I α.

marking_scheme.step: I, τ and L as counterparts

questions.stem_md: Define the radius of gyration of a body. Using the standard values of the moment of inertia, find its value for a thin ring and for a uniform disc, each of radius $R$, about the central axis.

answer.model_answer_md: The radius of gyration $k$ of a body of mass $M$ is the distance from the axis at which the whole mass could be concentrated to give the same moment of inertia, so $I = Mk^2$ and $k = \sqrt{I/M}$. answer.model_answer_md: A particle of mass $m_i$ at distance $r_i$ from the axis moves in a circle with speed $v_i = r_i\omega$, the same $\omega$ for every particle of a rigid body.
